name: Jamal Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Jamal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to companies, unions or parties, and what you say is confidential. Tell me about a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead installer for Northline Modular. They build timber wall and floor panels in a factory on the ring road, and my crew of five puts them together on site, a three-storey block of flats in about two weeks. My day is crane lifts, bolting, sealing joints and checking everything is plumb, which means straight up and down. I love it when a whole floor goes up before lunch. I hate standing in the wind waiting for a lorry that's stuck in traffic.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does technology come into it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All over the place. I use an AI app every morning to check the lift sequence against the drawings, and I've got it reading the delivery notes so I know which panel is on which lorry. I live on my own in a studio flat, so my costs are low, but the pay's on the low side too and I've never got much more than a few weeks put by. I spend too much on gadgets, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: First picture. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and people got carried away. On site I'd keep showing the lads how I use it for the lift plans. Online I'd probably post a video of a floor going up in a morning, because that's the real tech story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I stay on lower pay doing a job I'm very good at. Northline pays less than the big contractors because they say modular is quicker, so we should do more for less. Nothing changing just means that argument carries on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Northline and ask about moving into the factory as a production planner, since I know both ends. I'd stop buying gadgets for a bit and try to get two months saved. And I'd keep sharpening how I use AI, because it's the only edge I've got that the others haven't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit restless. I'm not scared of anything in this one. I just want more than this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Northline pays less because modular is quicker. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It winds me up, because quicker is down to us, not the panels. My crew is fast because I've worked out every lift. If they paid by the floor, we'd be well paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gadget would you not buy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a new drone I've been eyeing for site photos, about six hundred. I'd hold off and use my phone. That's six hundred towards my two months.

say: I'd say AI is a **decent tool** and people got carried away.
Online I'd post a floor going up in a morning, the **real tech story**.
think: I think I stay on **lower pay** for a job I'm very good at.
Northline argues **modular is quicker**, so we should do more for less.
do: Ask about a **production planner** role in the Northline factory.
Skip the **six-hundred drone** and save two months.
Keep **sharpening my AI use** as my edge on site.
feel: I feel **restless** and a bit uneasy, wanting **more than this**.
S0.quote: Northline pays less than the big contractors because they say modular is quicker, so we should do more for less.
fieldNote: Jamal's grievance is that his crew's **speed isn't paid**.
He already uses AI **daily** and treats it as his edge.
He's restless, not afraid, and thinking of the **factory side**.
He'd give up the **drone purchase** to build savings.

steps.text: Ask Northline about a production planner role in the factory
Hold off on the six-hundred drone and save it
Use the AI app to tighten every lift plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for modular, because the whole thing is built on planning, and AI is great at planning. I'd tell the crew to get comfortable with tablets. I'd probably post about it, the factory side is about to get really interesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's mostly good for me, as long as I move. Northline's planners and estimators shrink, because AI does their job, but someone has to run the AI and fix its mistakes on site. That could be me, I already catch its mistakes every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Northline to make me the person who checks the AI's lift plans and delivery schedules across all their sites. I'd look into a short course in construction digital tools at the college. If Northline didn't bite, I'd look at the bigger modular firms in the city, even if it meant moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, a little uneasy. I like this kind of change. I just don't want to be the guy who sees it coming and still misses the bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving to the city mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leaving my studio and my mum's Sunday dinners, mainly. I've got no partner or kids, so it's simpler for me than for most. Rent's higher there, though, and I've got next to no savings for the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, probably, he's been bolting panels for fifteen years and hates his phone. He's a great installer. I'd want to bring him along rather than leave him behind.

I'd tell the crew to get **comfortable with tablets**.
think: I think it's good for me **as long as I move**.
Planners shrink, but someone must **run the AI** and fix its mistakes on site.
do: Ask Northline to make me the **AI plan checker** across their sites.
Take a short **digital tools course** at the college.
Look at **city modular firms** if Northline doesn't bite.
feel: I feel **mostly excited**, but uneasy about **missing the bus**.
S1.quote: I don't want to be the guy who sees it coming and still misses the bus.
fieldNote: Jamal sees himself as the natural **AI checker** because he already catches its errors.
He'd **move to the city** if needed, freer than most with no partner or kids.
He'd bring along **Gary**, a veteran installer who hates his phone.
His main fear is **hesitating**, not the technology.

steps.text: Pitch a cross-site AI plan checking role to Northline
Take a short construction digital tools course at the college
Apply to modular firms in the city if Northline says no

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the fast one. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready, this is the real thing, and I'd be posting about how to adapt. At work I'd tell the crew the robots aren't here yet, but the planning side is about to change overnight. I'd want to be a calm voice, not a scary one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's tighter than I'd like. By 2028 all the planning and checking I'm proud of is done by AI, so my edge is gone. Then about 2031 the robots can do the installing too, and I'd be 31 with almost no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd try to get into the factory side, because that's where the robots will be built and run first. I'd go straight to the college for anything on robot operation or maintenance. I'd cut back hard on spending and save every bit I can, and I'd move if a better job was in the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd be moving, not frozen. The speed is the bit that scares me. I can learn fast, but not that fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots mean for your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my brain stops being special in 2028 but my hands keep paying until about 2031. So those three years are about getting into the robot side before the robots arrive. The worst thing would be to sit on site enjoying the last good years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I might move to the city and that money might be tight for a year. She'd tell me to come home if it goes wrong. I'd tell her I would, which is half true.

say: I'd say **get ready**, this is the real thing.
I'd tell the crew the **planning side** changes overnight, though robots aren't here yet.
think: I think by **2028** my planning edge is gone.
Around **2031** robots install too, and I'd be 31 with almost no savings.
do: Move into the **factory side**, where robots are built and run first.
Take any **robot operation** or maintenance course at the college.
Cut spending hard and **move to the city** for a better job.
feel: I feel **anxious but moving**, scared most by **the speed**.
S2.quote: My brain stops being special in 2028 but my hands keep paying until about 2031.
fieldNote: Jamal sees his **planning edge** as the first thing lost.
He uses the **three-year gap** to get into the robot side early.
His warning to himself: don't **enjoy the last good years** on site.
He's free to **move**, but has almost no savings to do it.

steps.text: Apply for a job in the Northline panel factory
Enrol on the college's robot operation and maintenance course
Cancel gadget spending and save every spare pound
Move to the city for a modular robot role if offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a great head start for anyone who uses it. I'd be posting tips for site people on learning the new tools. At work I'd push Northline to train us on the robots before they arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I could get ahead of this. AGI by 2031, robots around 2034, so I'd be 34 and could have three or four years in the factory side by then. That's not a bad place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year learning everything about the robots Northline is testing in the factory. I'd take a proper course, maybe in mechatronics, which is mechanics plus electronics, part-time. I'd save, and only move once I knew which firm was serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but hopeful. I like this one. It's fast enough to matter and slow enough to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Mechatronics is a big step. Can you afford a course like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it's part-time and cheap, or if Northline pays. I'd ask them, because they'd want someone who knows both the site and the machines. If not, I'd do an online course and pay monthly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a chance you're too confident?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. My mum says I always think I'll land on my feet. But I've seen the robots at the trade show, and they still need someone who knows what a good joint looks like.

say: I'd say five years is a **great head start** for anyone who uses it.
I'd push Northline to **train us on robots** before they arrive.
think: I think I could **get ahead** of this with factory experience by 34.
It's fast enough to matter and **slow enough to plan**.
do: Learn everything about the **robots Northline is testing**.
Take a part-time **mechatronics course**, mechanics plus electronics.
Save, and **move only** once I know which firm is serious.
feel: I feel **uneasy but hopeful**, and I like this one.
S3.quote: I've seen the robots at the trade show, and the robots still need someone who knows what a good joint looks like.
fieldNote: Jamal sees five years as the **sweet spot**: fast enough to matter, slow enough to plan.
He'd ask Northline to **fund mechatronics** training.
He admits he might be **too confident**, as his mum says.
His confidence rests on robots still needing **site judgement**.

steps.text: Learn the robots Northline is testing in its factory
Ask Northline to fund a part-time mechatronics course
Save two months before considering a move to the city

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, there's no excuse not to be ready. I'd tell the crew to learn one new thing a year. Online I'd say construction could be a great job again if we get this right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel good about it. I'd be 37 when the robots arrive around 2039, and by then I could be running a robot crew. The thinking side changes by 2036, but I'd already have moved into the machine side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep my crew going and keep using AI daily. I'd start a part-time course in robotics and save towards a deposit. I'd move to the factory side when the timing is right, not in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually, and quite excited. This is the one where I come out ahead. The only thing that'd worry me is if I got lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would running a robot crew actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me and two others on site, three or four machines doing the lifting and bolting, and us checking joints and fixing problems. Fewer people, better paid, I hope. I'd want Gary in that crew if he'd learn the tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years that you wouldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save, buy a flat maybe, and take my time picking the right course. With two years I'd jump at anything. With ten, I'd pick properly.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty**, so there's no excuse.
I'd say construction could be a **great job again** if we get this right.
think: I think I could be **running a robot crew** by 37.
I'd already be on the **machine side** when thinking work changes in 2036.
do: Keep my crew going and use **AI daily**.
Start a part-time **robotics course** and save for a deposit.
Move to the **factory side** when the timing is right.
feel: I feel **calm** and quite **excited**, worried only about getting lazy.
S4.quote: Me and two others on site, three or four machines doing the lifting and bolting, and us checking joints and fixing problems.
fieldNote: Jamal sees this as **the one where he comes out ahead**.
He pictures a **small robot crew** with fewer, better-paid people.
Ten years lets him **pick properly** instead of jumping at anything.
His only fear is **getting lazy** with so much time.

steps.text: Keep running the install crew while using AI every day
Start a part-time robotics course at the college
Save towards a deposit on a flat
Move to Northline's factory side when the timing is right

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to jump with no savings and no time to pick the right course. What would help is firms like Northline training their own crews on the robots, and cheap part-time courses you can do while still working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about pay. Everyone thinks robots mean lower pay, but if the crews that run them are small and skilled, they could be paid properly. That's the future I'd want to build.

headlineQuote: If the crews that run construction robots are small and skilled, they could be paid properly.
portrait: Jamal is 27, **lead installer** for a modular builder, putting up factory-made panels on site.
He lives alone, uses AI **every day** for lift plans, and has only a few weeks saved.
He's **adaptive** and practical, and sees the factory and robot side as his future.
Fast AGI makes him **anxious** because his planning edge goes first.
With ten years he's **calm**, picturing himself running a robot crew.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most: he'd have to **jump with no savings** and little time.
whatWouldHelp: Firms **training their own crews** on robots.
